checkpoints: Centralize the users domain in one key factory, hierarchical general-to-specific: users.all=["users"], users.list(filters)=["users","list",filters], users.detail(id)=["users","detail",id] — that ordering is exactly what lets invalidateQueries({queryKey:["users"]}) prefix-match and sweep every query in the domain.
createUser invalidates the users.list subtree (a new member can appear in any filtered list) but not any detail, since no detail page could exist for a user that didn't exist yet.
deleteUser invalidates both users.list (membership/content changed) and users.detail(id) for the removed record, so an open detail page reflects the user is gone.

updateUser invalidates users.detail(id) (detail changed) and the users.list subtree, because the user's fields also render inside lists — skipping list invalidation would leave lists stale even though detail is correct.
Every variable that affects a query's result (filters, page, id) belongs in the key since the key IS the cache's identity; never put a function or unstable object reference in the key.
Too-flat keys (no filters/detail split) let one invalidation kick out detail when only a list changed, and cause two lists with different filters to collide directly in the cache by sharing a key.

Too-fine keys (separate ad-hoc constants per filter combo, not routed through the factory) force each mutation to manually enumerate every existing list variant to invalidate — easy to miss one, same mismatch bug.

Default strategy: invalidate the whole ["users"] prefix on any mutation (costing a few extra refetches on rarely-mounted lists, cheaper than a stale row), narrowing only once profiling shows a refetch storm — and the factory itself is the deliverable, since importing from one place prevents differently-shaped keys for the same domain.

States the core contract rule as two atomic signals: `nextCursor` is the sole "keep going" signal, and `null` is the sole "exhausted" signal — the client never needs a separate total-count or error code to know when to stop.
States the concrete request/response shape: `GET /feed?cursor=<anchor>&limit=<n>` returns `{ data: Item[], nextCursor }`.

States the cursor anchors to a stable position (an id, timestamp, or end-index) rather than a raw absolute offset, because inserts/removals between loads make an offset drift into duplicated or skipped items.

States the cursor is opaque to the client — the client only echoes back the exact value the server gave it, never parses or computes on it, so the server stays free to change the encoding without breaking any client.
States that blocking an abusive page size is the server's job, never the client's — e.g. clamping `limit` into a hard bound such as `Math.max(1, Math.min(50, limit))`.

States the client hook mapping: an `initialPageParam` seeds the first cursor, `queryFn` sends the `pageParam` back as `cursor`, and `getNextPageParam` reads `nextCursor` from the page that just finished.

States the hasNextPage/loop-control behavior: a real `nextCursor` value keeps `hasNextPage` true and the loader armed, `null` flips it false and stops auto-loading, and guarding a double in-flight fetch (`hasNextPage && !isFetchingNextPage`) is the client's own responsibility, not the contract's.

States the trade-off: cursor pagination gives up jumping straight to an arbitrary page N and requires a stable sort key — worth it for a live feed to never duplicate or skip an item, but a mostly-static table needing random page jumps (e.g. admin numbered pagination) is better served by offset (skip/take).
These three steps are just three different states of ONE cache entry, not three separate stories.

Step 1 (first mount): the sidebar and main panel both register interest in the same empty entry, so exactly one queryFn call runs and both render from that single write — exactly ONE request despite two call sites.

Step 2 (navigate away and back within 10 seconds): still under the 30-second staleTime so the entry is fresh; re-mounting both components returns cached data immediately without calling queryFn — ZERO requests, the list appears instantly with no skeleton.

Step 3 (switch tabs and come back a minute later): past the 30-second staleTime threshold so the entry is now stale; the focus event triggers a background refetch, but the old data stays on screen with no skeleton while isFetching quietly flips on and off once the fresh data arrives — stale-while-revalidate.

The deep reason: useQuery isn't a fetch call, it's a subscription into a shared cache keyed by queryKey — the component never decides whether to call the API, the cache decides based on whether data exists yet and whether it's fresh or stale.

This "surprisingly few requests" arithmetic only holds if both call sites genuinely share the same entry — an unstable queryKey or a recreated QueryClient (losing the singleton) breaks the sharing and all three predictions fall apart.
onMutate runs before the request is sent and cancels the in-flight refetches on that query key.
onMutate snapshots the current cached value, for use as a rollback point.
onMutate writes "liked" directly into the cache — because the UI renders from the cache, the heart flips instantly without waiting for the 600ms round-trip.
The snapshot is returned as context so this specific mutation keeps its own copy, avoiding confusion if another mutation runs in parallel.
On the 200 branch, nothing else visibly changes when the response arrives; onSettled invalidates the key and a background GET confirms the value holds.
On the 500 branch, the mutation function throws and onError restores the old snapshot into the cache, so the heart un-flips to the prior state.

On the 500 branch, onError also fires a danger toast so the user knows the like didn't stick — without it, the user would just see the heart go dark with no explanation and likely blame themselves rather than the server.

Regardless of branch, onSettled always invalidates so the cache re-syncs with the server's truth — network latency becomes invisible to the user while correctness stays insured by the snapshot/rollback pair.
The refetch is not waste — it's exactly the step that makes the server the arbiter of truth.
A hand-pushed record carries a client-fabricated id and skips server normalization.
A hand-pushed record also skips concurrent edits made by other clients entirely.
The more mutation kinds exist (create/update/delete), the more splice codepaths must each be remembered separately, and missing just one silently shows the wrong thing.
invalidateQueries declares the dependency once — any successful write marks the list stale and the active query refetches on its own.
That refetch converges the UI to the server's truth at the cost of just one GET round trip.

Choose the direct/optimistic write only when perceived latency genuinely matters (a like, an inline rename, a fast toggle) — and then treat it as an "insured guess": snapshot the cache before writing, roll back on error, invalidate on settle to reconcile.
Default to invalidate; only upgrade to optimistic when truly needed, and the upgrade must carry the full snapshot/rollback/reconcile contract, not just the direct write alone.
Offset (skip/take) means "give me rows 20-29" based on absolute position.
If rows are inserted at the top since the previous load, the next offset page re-shows items already seen (duplicates).
If rows are deleted, an item can vanish before the user ever saw it (a skip).
The problem is correctness, not performance — skip position is only accurate at the moment it was computed and doesn't survive concurrent changes.

A cursor instead says "continue right after this anchor" (an id, timestamp, or end index like nextCursor), anchoring to data rather than position, so it survives inserts/deletes elsewhere in the list.
The consuming side is simpler: the client just reads nextCursor and stops when it's null — no need to know total record count or do page math.

Offset is still the honest choice for a static/near-unchanging dataset or for UX needing "jump straight to page N" (admin tables, numbered search results), because a cursor only walks forward sequentially and can't do random access.

The cursor's cost is needing a genuinely stable, non-colliding, never-changing ordering key — so the choice follows the access pattern: volatile/append-heavy/continuously-scrolled feed → cursor; stable table accessed randomly by page → offset.

Optimistic is a per-interaction trade, not an app-wide setting, because it changes what the cache is allowed to say — for the window between onMutate's write and onSettled's invalidate, the cache holds an unconfirmed value (a deliberate, on-credit lie).

That credit is only safe under a strict contract: cancel in-flight queries first (so a stale refetch can't overwrite the guess), snapshot the prior value before writing (so onError has something exact to restore), write the optimistic value, then reconcile via invalidate on settle regardless of outcome.
Optimistic is worth it for likes, toggles, renames — the result is easy to guess, the write is effectively idempotent, and a rare rollback barely bothers the user.

Optimistic must be refused for payments, sending a message/email, or any action whose outcome the server computes and the client cannot guess — showing "sent"/"paid" then silently un-sending is worse than a one-second spinner, and a non-idempotent write can double-apply on a delayed retry before failure is even visible.
Invariant 1: the mutation function must throw on a non-ok response — one that swallows the error and resolves normally means onError (and rollback) never runs, leaving the UI stuck on a lie.

Invariant 2: retry must be a deliberate choice, not a framework default — an enabled retry delays the rollback the user is waiting to see, and for non-idempotent calls risks re-sending the same write.
A rollback must never be silent — onError reverting the cache must also surface a toast, since a value quietly changing back erodes trust more than an honest spinner.
The overall answer to the PM: pessimistic stays the default everywhere, with optimistic reserved for the highest-frequency, lowest-stakes interactions under this contract.
The 201 clears the server — the bug is entirely client-side, in the cache wiring.
useQuery registers the list under queryKey: ["users"].
On success, addMutation calls qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["user"] }) — singular, not plural.

invalidateQueries matches cache entries by comparing keys; since ["user"] matches nothing in the cache, the ["users"] entry is never marked stale, so the active query has no reason to refetch, and the UI keeps rendering the pre-mutation snapshot until a hard reload cold-fetches the list.

This is exactly why the failure is silent: a queryKey mismatch throws no exception and logs no warning — invalidateQueries simply does nothing when nothing matches, letting this bug slip past code review.
The fix: invalidate ["users"] to match the query exactly.
To prevent future drift, export the key from one shared factory (e.g. queryKeys.users) that both useQuery and every mutation touching that list import.

To prove it: repeat the add-user flow, watch the Network tab for the chained GET /users right after the POST, confirm the new row renders without a reload, and check in the query devtools that the entry flips stale → fetching → fresh.
Both symptoms trace back to the same spot: the statement order inside onMutate.
onError does run and does correctly call qc.setQueryData(USERS_KEY, ctx.previous) — the rollback code itself isn't missing or broken.

But onMutate calls the optimistic setQueryData FIRST and only calls getQueryData AFTER, so by snapshot time the cache already holds the optimistic (about-to-fail) value, not the original one — the actual root cause of symptom 1.
ctx.previous is therefore the failed data itself, so the "rollback" is just writing that failed value back onto itself — a no-op dressed up as a rollback.

Symptom 2's root cause: the code is entirely missing await qc.cancelQueries({ queryKey: USERS_KEY }); if a GET /users is already in flight (from staleness or a focus refetch), it can resolve right after the optimistic write runs and overwrite the cache with stale data for a moment before onSettled's invalidate fixes it again — that is exactly the success-path flicker.

Fix: restore the fixed three-step order — await cancelQueries first, then getQueryData snapshot while the cache is still intact, then setQueryData so the UI changes immediately; return { previous } so each concurrently-running mutation owns its own snapshot via ctx; onSettled keeps its final invalidate step unchanged.
Verify symptom 1: force the fail flag and assert the name reverts exactly to the baseline (mirrors Flow 2).
Verify symptom 2: perform two rapid sequential edits and assert the final result is last-write-wins with no intermediate flicker (mirrors Flow 3).

Most severe finding (correctness): new QueryClient() lives in the component body — every render constructs a brand-new, completely empty cache store, so any previously fetched data vanishes, no other component can subscribe to the same entry, and Strict Mode's double-render makes it visibly worse right away.
Fix for that: move creation to a lazy useState(() => new QueryClient(...)) at the app root so the client lives exactly once for the app's whole lifetime — not wrapped around this page's own subtree.
Moderately severe finding (UX): the skeleton renders off query.isFetching, but isFetching is true during EVERY background revalidation, not just the first load.
So after each invalidation or every time the tab regains focus, the user's perfectly good list gets replaced by a skeleton flash, defeating stale-while-revalidate entirely.
Fix by binding the skeleton to isPending (never had data) and, if a refresh signal is wanted, adding a small non-blocking indicator on isFetching && !isPending.
Verify: run under Strict Mode and confirm the cache isn't reset (exactly one entry in devtools).
Verify: add a test asserting a refetch never makes the already-loaded list disappear.
